product.title: Swedish 103 - B1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from A2 to a solid B1 in Swedish. Each unit has two dialogues set during Dian's six-month internship in Göteborg — at the office, at the tax agency, at the health center, at a family dinner — with word-for-word translations, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. The hardest spots of the level each get a full unit: the pluperfect and modal + perfect (skulle ha, borde ha), strong verbs grouped by vowel family, sentence adverbs in long sentences, participles that agree like adjectives, choosing between the s-passive and bli, unreal conditions, reported speech, and the fixed prepositions that turn tänka into tänka på.

blocks.text: If you have worked through **Svenska 102**, you can already do a great deal in Swedish. You can tell the story of your weekend, use particle verbs like *komma ihåg* and *stänga av*, read a sign that says *Dörren stängs kl. 18*, say what you would do *om du vann en miljon*, and report what someone else said. That is the A2 toolkit, and it carries you through most of daily life. What it does not do yet is let you **work**, argue, explain a problem at the tax office, or write a letter that a Swede would read without smiling.

That is what B1 is for. The Council of Europe calls it the "threshold" level, and the name fits: this is where you stop being a visitor in the language and become an independent user of it. In practice, B1 means **longer sentences**. You will learn to stack the past in three layers (*jag flyttade*, *jag har flyttat*, *jag hade flyttat*), to talk about what *should have* or *might have* happened (*jag borde ha frågat*, *han kan ha missat tåget*), to put a whole subordinate clause first and still keep the verb in second place, and to move words like *inte*, *alltid* and *nog* to the right spot in every kind of clause.

The vocabulary grows up too. B1 is the Swedish of adult life: a sublet contract for a room *i andra hand*, a letter from the landlord, a visit to *Skatteverket*, a phone call to the health center, a meeting where nobody says no directly. Two things will occupy you more than any grammar table: **fixed prepositions** (Swedes *tänker på*, *väntar på*, are *intresserade av* and *nöjda med* — and the preposition is rarely the one English would choose) and **compound words**, which Swedish builds as freely as German and which you will learn to take apart at a glance.

The story moves west. **Dian** has finished her second year in Stockholm, and at the end of August she starts a six-month internship (*praktik*) at a small design and IT company at **Lindholmen**, on the north bank of the river in **Göteborg**. Her boss is **Karin**, her closest colleagues are **Mattias** and **Leila** (who grew up in Göteborg), and their most demanding client is a textile company in **Borås**. She sublets a room in the old harbor district of **Majorna** from **Hanna**, who is working in Berlin. Along the way Dian calls the health center about a fever that won't go away, has her bike stolen, registers her new address with *Skatteverket*, and discovers how a Swedish meeting really works. She spends weekends in the archipelago with **Oskar**, goes back for dinner with his parents in **Askim** — she first met them two years ago — and phones **Elin** in Stockholm whenever something happens. Halfway through, after three months, Karin gives her a project of her own; in the last units the internship is ending in February, Dian thinks about moving back to Stockholm, and she writes a real job application — and so will you.

Each unit now has **two dialogues** instead of one, so plan on about forty minutes per sitting. One unit every three days takes you through the book in about two months. Göteborgers are famous for their puns and their dry humor; by the end of this course you should be able to understand the jokes, even if you are not yet telling them. *Nu kör vi!* — Let's go!

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: The method has not changed since Svenska 101, but the units are bigger. Each one has **two dialogues**, usually showing the same grammar from two angles — once at work and once in Dian's private life. Do both in one sitting if you can, about **40 minutes**; if not, split the unit in two and finish it the next day.
Work through each unit in this order:

items: **Dialogues** — read each one out loud first, without the translation. At B1 you will understand more than you expect from context alone; trust that before you check.

**Literal translation** — still there under every line. At this level it shows you less about single words and more about **word order**: where the verb sits, where *inte* lands, what gets moved to the front. Read it for the shape of the sentence.
**Notes and grammar** — the notes explain what is new in that line; the grammar boxes give you the system behind it. Read the tables with a pencil, not just your eyes.
**Vocabulary** — nouns still come with *en* or *ett*. Verbs and adjectives that take a fixed preposition are always listed **with** it (*vänta på*, *nöjd med*). Learn them as one piece.
**Exercises** — write your answers by hand. In translation items your sentence may differ from the key and still be right; compare word order and endings, not word choice.
**Answer key** — only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: Every unit starts by sending you back to an earlier unit — sometimes in this book, sometimes in Svenska 101 or 102. Cover the Swedish, look at the English, and rebuild the sentences. At B1 the goal is speed: you should be able to say them almost without thinking.
Keep **one notebook page for fixed prepositions** and one for **strong verbs**. Add to them in every unit. By Unit 20 they will be your own grammar book.

blocks.text: Two habits make the biggest difference at this level. First, **shadowing**: read a dialogue line aloud, then say it again without looking, at the same speed and with the same melody. Second, **retelling**: after each dialogue, tell what happened in three or four Swedish sentences, in the past tense, out loud. That is exactly what a B1 speaker is expected to do.

You know the sounds of Swedish already. At B1 the challenge is **rhythm**: longer words, longer sentences, and words that run into each other in natural speech. This short chapter covers the three things that matter most. Respellings follow the same rules as in Svenska 101 and 102 — capital letters mark the stressed syllable.
Stress in compound words

A Swedish compound has **one main stress**, on the stressed syllable of its **first** part, and it always takes tone 2, the singing melody. The last part keeps a lighter, secondary stress. That rhythm tells a listener that the word is one word, and it can change the meaning:

head: Written
Say it
Meaning
rows: a big city (two words, main stress on *stad*)
a metropolis (one word, main stress on *stor*)
personal ID number (stress stays where *person* has it)

blocks.text: Long official words look frightening on paper but are easy once you hear them as a chain of short ones with one strong beat at the start: *arbetsmiljöverket* → **AHR-behts-mil-yö-verk-et**, "the work-environment authority".
Stress in particle verbs

In a particle verb, the **particle** takes the stress and the verb goes almost flat. When the particle is fused onto the front of the word — in participles and many formal verbs — the stress moves with it to the front.

Stress can be the only thing that tells two sentences apart. *Jag tycker **OM** honom* means "I like him"; *Vad **TYCKER** du om honom?* means "What do you think of him?" — the same *om*, but unstressed, is simply "about".
When r meets s, t, d, n across words

You learned in Svenska 101 that *rs* inside a word becomes "sh" (*först* → **fösht**). In natural speech the same thing happens **across word boundaries**: a word ending in *-r* melts into the next word if it starts with *s, t, d, n* or *l*. The *r* disappears and the next consonant is said with the tongue curled back.

blocks.title: Don't overdo it
items: You do not have to produce these blends to be understood — a clear *r* followed by a clear *s* is perfectly fine. But you do have to **recognize** them, because that is how Karin, Mattias and Leila will speak to Dian.
Not every Swede blends. In **Skåne**, in the far south, the *r* is made at the back of the throat and never melts into the next sound. You will meet that accent, and others, in Svenska 104.

blocks.text: Swedish uses the perfect more often than American English does: *Har du sett filmen?* — "Did you see the movie?" As soon as you name a past time, though, switch to the past: *Jag såg den i fredags.*

blocks.text: Talking about the future (Unit 6)
Adverbs of probability: *antagligen*, *troligen*, *förmodligen* (probably), *kanske* (maybe), *säkert* (surely, most likely).
Word order: the sentence frame (Units 3, 4)

blocks.title: The two rules that do most of the work
items: **Main clause:** whatever comes first — subject, object, time, a whole subordinate clause — the finite verb comes **second**. Sentence adverbs (*inte, aldrig, alltid, kanske, nog, redan, ofta*) follow the verb, or the subject if it has been pushed behind the verb.
**Subordinate clause:** no inversion, and sentence adverbs go **before** the finite verb: *...att hon **inte** kommer*.

blocks.text: Reflexive and reciprocal (Unit 8)

head: Form
Rule
Example
rows: "his/her/their own": refers to the subject of the **same clause**
Dian ringde **sin** mamma. · Leila tror att hon har glömt **sin** nyckel.
someone else, or inside the subject itself
Dian sa att **hennes** mamma hade ringt.

blocks.text: Participles as adjectives (Units 7, 9)

The **present participle** ends in *-ande* (or *-ende* after a long vowel) and never changes: *en spännande film*, *ett leende barn*, *de boende i huset*. The **past participle** agrees like an adjective:
Particle verbs: separate or fused (Unit 7)
Participles are always fused. Some fused verbs mean something different from the separate version, and the fused one is usually more formal.
No double definite (Unit 10)

Tåget var sent, **vilket** betydde att jag missade mötet.

blocks.text: **Det** as an empty subject: *det finns* (there is), *det står i brevet* (it says in the letter), *det regnar*. A **cleft sentence** puts the focus on one part: *Det var Karin som ringde* — "It was Karin who called."

blocks.text: Reported speech (Unit 15)
Compound words (Unit 17)
The **last** part decides the meaning and the gender: *en arbetsplats* is a kind of *plats*, *ett skrivbord* a kind of *bord*.

Two lists that every B1 learner keeps going back to. The first groups the most important **strong verbs** by their vowel pattern, as in Unit 2 — learn one verb per family well, and the others follow the same tune. The second lists **verbs and adjectives with fixed prepositions** from Unit 16 and across the book.
Strong verbs by vowel family

Families are a strong tendency, not a law: *sjunga* (*sjöng*, *sjungit*) and *skjuta* (*sköt*, *skjutit*) keep the vowel of the infinitive in the supine, and *ligga* (*låg*, *legat*) belongs to no family at all. Note that strong verbs have no ending in the past: *skrev*, *drack*, *flög* — never *skrevde*.
Verbs and adjectives with fixed prepositions

head: Swedish
English
Example
rows: Jag har inte råd **med** en bil.
Jag är inte van **vid** mörkret än.

blocks.title: How to learn them
items: Never learn the verb or the adjective alone. Learn **vänta på** as one word, the way you learned *en bok* rather than *bok*.
When the preposition is followed by a verb, add **att**: *Jag är trött på att vänta.* · *Hon är bra på att presentera.*

blocks.text: You have reached the end of B1. You can follow a meeting, explain a problem on the phone, read a letter from an authority with a dictionary at your side, tell a long story in three layers of the past, and write a job application. Most Swedes will now stay in Swedish with you — and that changes everything, because from here on, every conversation is practice.
Three things waiting for you at B2

items: **The architecture of the sentence.** At B1 you learned where the verb and *inte* go. At B2 you learn **what to put first** — how Swedes move known information to the front and new information to the end, and why that makes a text flow.

**Attitude in small words.** *Ju*, *väl*, *nog*, *liksom*, *typ*, *asså* — the little words that make a sentence sound friendly, ironic, impatient or unsure. You met some of them at A2; at B2 you learn to use them on purpose, together with spoken slang and the difference between spoken and written Swedish.

**Formal and regional Swedish.** Nominal style in news and official texts (*den av regeringen föreslagna lagen*), claims and sources in the media (*han ska ha sagt*), idioms like *ingen ko på isen*, and the accents of Skåne, Norrland and Finland — plus how much Norwegian and Danish you can already understand.

blocks.text: Habits for the next step

items: **Listen to the news every day.** Sveriges Radio's *Klartext* gives you the day's news in clear, slower Swedish; when that feels easy, move on to *Ekot*. Ten minutes a day is enough.
**Read one real text a week.** An article from a Swedish newspaper, a page of a novel, a report from your own field. Underline every fixed preposition and every compound word you can take apart.
**Write.** A short diary entry, an email, a comment under an article. Writing is where the word order of long sentences really settles.
**Volunteer to speak.** Join a *språkcafé*, a study circle, or a club. At B1 you no longer need a teacher in the room — you need people and topics.

blocks.title: A note about praktik
items: If you ever get the chance to do an internship or a job in Sweden, take it. Nothing teaches the language of fika, meetings and email faster — and nothing teaches *lagom* better than a Swedish office.
Your new lifesaver sentence: **"Kan du säga det på ett annat sätt?"** — "Can you say that another way?" It keeps the conversation in Swedish without pretending you understood.

blocks.text: *Tack för att du har följt med Dian ända till Göteborg. Vi ses i Svenska 104!* — Thanks for following Dian all the way to Göteborg. See you in Svenska 104!
